articles.title: Earth likely made its own oceans during formation, not by comet bombardment
articles.description: For decades, the origin of Earth's oceans has been framed as a cosmic delivery service. The prevailing theory suggested that water arrived on the young, scorched planet via a relentless bombardment of icy comets and meteorites from the frigid outer reaches of the solar system. However, new evidence suggests that Earth may not have been a passive recipient of water, but rather its own manufacturer. Researchers from the University of New Mexico have proposed a mechanism where water was an inevitable byproduct of the planet's formation. During the process of pebble accretion-where Earth grew by collecting small rocky particles-the planet was enveloped in a dense, hydrogen-rich atmosphere under extreme heat. In this environment, the chemistry of the surface transformed the atmosphere into a planetary-scale water factory. To test this, a team led by PhD student Susmita Garay and Professor Zachary Sharp simulated the conditions of the early Earth in a laboratory. They exposed silicate rocks to temperatures ranging from 1,200 to 1,400 degrees Celsius within an environment of pure hydrogen. The result was a precise chemical reaction: hydrogen from the atmosphere reacted with iron oxide present in the rocky debris. This process stripped the oxygen from the iron, converting it into metallic iron and releasing water vapor as a byproduct.
